claims.text: The simulated material is a single-crystal CoNiCrFeMn high-entropy-alloy nanowire deformed by molecular dynamics at 77, 300, and 1000 K.
Dislocation nucleation in the HEA initiates at free surfaces.
Dislocation nucleation does not initiate at vacancy clusters.
The nucleated defects are Shockley partial dislocations with Burgers vector 1/6<112>.
The partial dislocations glide on {111} planes and create intrinsic stacking faults.
The <110> orientation has a higher maximum yield strength than the <11-1> orientation.
The orientation dependence of yield strength is caused by differences in resolved shear stress on {111} slip planes.
The HCP-like regions are a percolating network of intrinsic stacking faults rather than a true FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Stacking-fault accumulation can unlock Lomer-Cottrell locks.
Interactions between moving partial dislocations form Lomer-Cottrell locks.
Lomer-Cottrell locks and stacking-fault networks hinder defect motion and contribute to work hardening.
Increasing temperature enhances thermal vibrations and lowers the activation barrier for dislocation nucleation.
Lowering the nucleation barrier at higher temperature increases dislocation density.
Yield strength decreases monotonically as temperature increases from 77 to 1000 K.
Dislocation density is highest at 77 K and decreases as temperature increases.
The apparent HCP fraction increases with strain and temperature.
The simulations use tensile strain rates between 10^8 and 10^10 s^-1.
The initial dislocation density is near zero.

Stacking faults can be distinguished from a true HCP phase because they show a continuous gradient of local order without a distinct HCP lattice-parameter shift, whereas a true transformation produces discrete lattice-parameter changes and a sharp HCP-related RDF peak.
A distinct HCP lattice parameter and sharp phase boundary would falsify the interpretation that the HCP-like regions are merely stacking faults.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says higher temperature increases dislocation density by lowering the nucleation barrier, while the predicted outcome says dislocation density is highest at 77 K and decreases with temperature.

The hypothesis denies a true FCC-to-HCP transformation, but the mechanism calls stacking-fault accumulation a martensitic-like transformation to HCP before reinterpreting it as percolation of stacking faults.
The material is called both FeNiCrMn, a four-element system, and CoCrFeMnNi/CoNiCrFeMn, a five-element system.
The initial state is framed as single-crystalline, whereas the boundary expands applicability to nanocrystalline material while also excluding samples with significant grain-boundary effects.
